newsitem.title: UK: UK fraud hotline hidden factor in jobless fall.
newsitem.headline: UK fraud hotline hidden factor in jobless fall.

text.p: A dramatic fall in British unemployment in the last two months may be partly a result of the launch of the government's new benefits fraud hotline, analysts said on Wednesday.
The hotline has received over 100,000 calls since its launch in August and a spokesman confirmed a large percentage of calls concerned people claiming unemployment benefit while working.

"The hotline appears to be succeeding in stopping people signing on. It affected the September unemployment figures by around 6,000 and looks like it has affected October too," said Philip Uglow, UK economist at Union Plc.
Unemployment fell by a massive 40,800 in October having fallen an upward revised 37,900 in September. In the previous six months, the monthly fall averaged 15,000 to 20,000.
The benefits hotline spokesman said there were no figures available on the outcome of investigations prompted by calls.
"It is too early to say, but all calls are all investigated, he said. He refused to comment on reports that up to 20,000 claimants have been stripped of their benefits.
But the Office for National Statistics noted that the number of existing claimants who failed to sign on for unemployment benefit in October was 17 percent higher than a year ago.
"The hotline may have had an effect, but other factors are also at work," said an ONS statistician.
On October 6, four days before the ONS made its monthly unemployment count, the government replaced unemployment benefit with the job seekers allowance which links benefit to active job search.

The ONS said it was too early for the new benefit to have had an impact on behaviour, but it estimated as much as 15,000 of the 40,800 fall in the jobless count in October could be due to operational changes at job centres rating claims.
"If that is the case it will bounce back by that number next month," said a statistician.
The ONS estimates the new allowance will reduce the claimant count by around 35,000 over the next six months.

"Distortions arising from the job seekers allowance and the new fraud hotline could cause unemployment data to overstate the true pace of tightening in the labour market in coming months," said Jonathan Loynes, UK economist at HSBC.
But other economists said earlier changes to the structure of benefits may be offsetting the impact of the job seekers allowance and fraud hotline.
In particular, tighter criteria for claiming invalidity benefit introduced last year mean thousands of claimants are still thought to be shifting onto the unemployment register.

David Mackie, UK economist at JP Morgan, said given this the unemployment figures may in fact be painting an accurate picture of the labour market, especially when the full range of unemployment and employment figures are taken together.

"The breadth of the figures show employment rising, especially manufacturing employment, job centre vacancies up and wages rising." He said this fits in with most other economic data showing a strong pick up in activity.
Manufacturing employment grew 13,000 in September after falling 6,000 in August, and in the three months to June employees in employment grew by 124,000.
